title: New Dish on the Menu
story: A café menu lists dishes from cheapest to most expensive. Prices are in cents, so 420 means 4.20, and two dishes can cost the same.
The cook adds a new dish. The printer needs to know which line it goes on so the menu stays sorted. If dishes already have that exact price, the new one goes before them, so it gets seen first.
task: Write insertPosition(prices, price). prices is sorted from smallest to largest and may contain repeats. Return the index where price should be inserted: the first index whose price is greater than or equal to price. If every price is smaller, return prices.length.
Do not change the list. An empty menu returns 0. Aim for O(log n).
constraints: prices is sorted in non-decreasing order.

examples.explanation: 350, 420 and 420 are cheaper than 500. The first price of 500 or more is 575, at index 3.
Two dishes already cost 420. The new one goes before both, at index 1. Index 3 would also keep the menu sorted, but the rule says before.

hints: In [350, 420, 420, 575, 890], mark each price as "smaller than 500" or "not". What shape does that row of marks have?
Because the list is sorted, it is always a block of "smaller" then a block of "not smaller". You want the first position of the second block.
Binary search for that boundary, not for a value. If the middle price is smaller than price, the boundary is to its right. Otherwise the middle might be the boundary, so keep it.
Start with lo = 0 and hi = n (the answer can be n). While lo < hi: if prices[mid] < price set lo = mid + 1, else hi = mid. When they meet, that is the answer.
bruteForce: Walk from the start and return the first index whose price is at least price, or n at the end. That takes O(n) time, which means up to 100,000 checks for each new dish.
A plain binary search that stops at the first equal price is wrong here: in the second example it first lands on index 2, one of the two 420s, and returns 2 instead of 1.

js: let lo = 0, hi = prices.length; // the answer is somewhere in [lo, hi]
if (prices[mid] < price) lo = mid + 1; // mid is too cheap: boundary is right of it
else hi = mid;                         // mid could be the boundary: keep it
py: lo, hi = 0, len(prices)  # the answer is somewhere in [lo, hi]
lo = mid + 1  # mid is too cheap: boundary is right of it
hi = mid  # mid could be the boundary: keep it
walkthrough: Search for a boundary, not a value: the first price that is not smaller than the new one.
• lo = 0, hi = 5, mid = 2. 420 is not smaller than 420, so index 2 might be the boundary. hi = 2.
• lo = 0, hi = 2, mid = 1. The price at index 1 is 420 again, so hi = 1.
• lo = 0, hi = 1, mid = 0. 350 < 420, so the boundary is to the right. lo = 1.

Two details matter. hi starts at n, not n - 1, because "after everything" is a valid answer. And when the middle is big enough you set hi = mid, not mid - 1, because the middle might be the answer. The loop still ends, since mid is always less than hi.
solution.timeWhy: The range [lo, hi] halves every round.
solution.spaceWhy: The algorithm only stores the two indexes lo and hi.
solution.takeaway: Many searches are really "find the first position where a yes/no condition turns true". Start with hi = n, set hi = mid when the condition holds and lo = mid + 1 when it does not. This lower-bound loop is the same as bisect_left in Python.
